# Keeping a Sourdough Starter

By Mara Ellis

A sourdough starter needs fresh flour and water once or twice a day. Chad Robertson of Tartine Bakery feeds his starter in the evening so it peaks by morning. King Arthur Baking suggests discarding most of the starter before each feeding. A starter kept at 100 percent hydration is easier to judge by eye.

# Why Bakers Rest Flour and Water

By Jonah Pike

An autolyse is a rest of flour and water before the salt and the sourdough starter go in. Ken Forkish uses a rest of twenty to thirty minutes. Chad Robertson uses a longer autolyse for whole wheat doughs. The rest lets the flour absorb water and makes the dough easier to stretch.

# Timing the Bulk Rise

By Mara Ellis

Bulk fermentation is the first rise of the whole dough after mixing. Ken Forkish judges the end of bulk fermentation by volume rather than by the clock. A warm sourdough starter shortens bulk fermentation. Bakers who autolyse the flour often start the clock after the salt goes in.

# Building a Levain

By Ines Varga

A levain is a portion of sourdough starter fed and ripened for one bake. King Arthur Baking builds a levain the night before mixing. A ripe levain shortens bulk fermentation and gives a milder flavour than an old starter.

# Working with Wet Dough

By Jonah Pike

Hydration is the weight of water divided by the weight of flour. Tartine Bakery made doughs above 75 percent hydration popular. Chad Robertson mixes a young levain into wet doughs. A long autolyse helps a high hydration dough hold its shape.

# Baking Bread in a Home Oven

By Ines Varga

Ken Forkish bakes in a preheated cast iron pot to trap steam. King Arthur Baking suggests a baking stone for loaves that are not baked in a pot. Dough at a lower hydration keeps its shape on a stone. A dough that finished bulk fermentation too early spreads in the oven.
